html:
A huge painted jar made in Athens around 760 to 750 BCE, taller than a person's waist, which stood over a woman's grave in the Dipylon cemetery, the Kerameikos. It is now in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

It is the best known work of the Geometric style. Bands of meanders, zigzags and other patterns cover the whole surface. In one band, the dead woman lies on a bier, and mourners with triangle bodies and stick arms raise their hands to their heads in grief. The painter, known only as the Dipylon Master, ran a workshop of such grave vases.

The vase comes from the century when Homer's poems were taking shape and the Greeks were adopting the alphabet. The human figures on it are some of the first in Greek art since the Bronze Age. Later Athenian potters turned to black-figure painting with fuller stories.
